title: Health Assessment & Nursing Skills: Lines, Tubes & Drains—IV, Urinary Catheter & Enteral Tube Safety
html:
Lines, tubes, and drains support treatment, nutrition, elimination, and recovery, but every device also creates risks: infection, pressure injury, obstruction, dislodgement, misconnections, bleeding, aspiration, and delayed recognition of deterioration. Safe nursing care begins with the client—not the equipment—and combines a stability check, purposeful device assessment, trend interpretation, action, and reassessment.

Learning goals

  • Assess the client before assessing a line, tube, or drain.
  • Use a consistent device sweep to verify indication, position, securement, connections, function, site condition, and client response.
  • Recognize infiltration, extravasation, phlebitis, infection, obstruction, migration, aspiration risk, and abnormal drainage.
  • Protect closed systems and use organization-approved infection-prevention practices.
  • Respond safely to urgent device complications without improvising an unverified intervention.
  • Document device findings, output, actions, communication, and reassessment.

Assess the client before the device

First assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, pain, and the reason the device is present. New respiratory distress, hypotension, altered mental status, rapidly increasing bleeding, severe pain, or sudden deterioration takes priority over completing a routine equipment checklist. Stabilize and activate the appropriate response while preventing further device-related harm.

Trace before use
Trace every tube from the client to its source or collection container. Confirm the prescribed route, solution, rate, suction setting, or drainage system; identify every connection; and resolve uncertainty before administering anything or reconnecting tubing.

Use a purposeful device sweep

For each device, verify the current order and indication, device type and anatomic location, insertion mark or visible external length when applicable, securement, dressing and surrounding tissue, tubing connections, clamps and prescribed settings, patency or expected function, output, and the client’s response. Compare with baseline and previous documentation. Ask whether the device is still necessary every day; unnecessary devices should be removed promptly through the appropriate order and policy pathway.

Perform hand hygiene and use Standard Precautions. Apply aseptic or sterile technique as required by the task and organization. Keep systems closed when designed to remain closed, disinfect access points according to policy, and avoid routine disconnection. Protect skin beneath tubing, hubs, stabilization devices, and collection equipment. Label tubing and trace it whenever accepting care, before use, after transport, and whenever a connection is uncertain.

Peripheral IV assessment

Assess the client, prescribed infusion, pump and rate, tubing, dressing, insertion site, limb, and distal neurovascular status as indicated. Ask about pain, burning, tightness, numbness, or leaking. Inspect and palpate according to policy for swelling, coolness, blanching, erythema, warmth, tenderness, induration, streaking, drainage, leakage, slowed flow, or repeated alarms. A missing blood return alone does not prove infiltration; interpret all findings together and never force a flush against resistance.

Infiltration is unintended leakage of a nonvesicant solution into tissue. Common cues include swelling, coolness, pallor or blanching, discomfort, leaking, and altered infusion flow. Stop the infusion, assess the site and limb, and follow the organization’s infiltration protocol, including catheter removal and compress or elevation instructions when applicable.

Extravasation is leakage of a vesicant or irritant capable of tissue injury. Pain, burning, swelling, tightness, color change, blistering, or an altered infusion can be early cues. Stop the infusion immediately and do not flush. Leave the vascular access device in place until the medication-specific protocol is reviewed because aspiration or an antidote may be required through it. Notify the appropriate provider and pharmacy resources, follow the extravasation protocol, and document and monitor the site.

Phlebitis may cause localized warmth, erythema, tenderness, induration, or a palpable venous cord. Purulent drainage, spreading erythema, fever, chills, or hemodynamic change raises concern for infection or systemic involvement. Stop use and follow policy for removal, culture, treatment, escalation, and alternate access.

Central vascular access

Identify the device and lumen purpose. Assess the dressing, securement, insertion site, exposed catheter or external-length reference, tubing, needleless connectors, and the client’s symptoms. Report new migration, damaged tubing, drainage, erythema, swelling, fever, chills, neck or arm swelling, chest discomfort, dyspnea, arrhythmia, or difficulty flushing. Do not advance a migrated catheter or use a line with uncertain tip position; secure it and follow the urgent verification pathway. Use central-line-specific policy for access, dressing care, blood sampling, flushing, and removal.

Indwelling urinary catheter safety

Verify an appropriate indication and reassess the need daily. Maintain a continuously closed drainage system and unobstructed flow. Secure the catheter, keep tubing free of kinks and dependent loops, position the bag below bladder level and off the floor, and prevent contact between the drainage spigot and a nonsterile container. Provide routine perineal hygiene; antiseptic cleansing is not recommended solely to prevent catheter-associated infection.

When urine output falls, assess the client first: hemodynamics, hydration clues, bladder symptoms or distention, recent output and trends. Then trace the tubing for kinks, compression, dependent loops, bag position, leakage, or visible obstruction. Do not irrigate automatically; follow the order and policy because routine bladder irrigation is not recommended. For a small fresh urine specimen such as a culture, disinfect the needleless sampling port and collect aseptically with the approved device—not from pooled urine in the drainage bag.

Cloudy or odorous urine alone does not establish a symptomatic urinary infection. Correlate urinary symptoms, fever or systemic findings, urinalysis or culture orders, and alternate explanations. Breaks, disconnections, or leakage compromise a closed system and require action according to policy.

Enteral tube assessment

Identify the tube and prescribed route, purpose, formula or medication, rate, flush plan, and whether gastric or post-pyloric placement is intended. Assess respiratory status, level of consciousness, swallowing and aspiration risk, nausea or vomiting, abdominal findings, bowel function, hydration, and feeding tolerance. Inspect the nose or stoma, securement, skin, tubing, connections, and visible external length.

Initial placement of a blindly inserted feeding tube is commonly verified radiographically before use. After that reference is established, compare external tube length and use the organization-approved verification method before feedings and medications and at required intervals. Coughing, vomiting, movement, loose securement, respiratory symptoms, or a changed external length can signal migration. Stop feeding or medication administration, assess breathing, and verify placement before reuse. Air-bolus auscultation—the “whoosh test”—and aspirate appearance alone are unreliable placement checks.

Keep the client positioned according to the order and aspiration-prevention policy during feeding and for the prescribed period afterward. Trace enteral tubing before connection, use enteral-only connectors, maintain prescribed flushes, and avoid mixing medications or formula without pharmacy and policy guidance. New respiratory distress, suspected aspiration, severe abdominal pain or distention, persistent vomiting, bleeding, or suspected displacement requires prompt escalation.

Surgical and wound drains

Verify the drain type, location, order, expected suction or gravity function, and baseline output. Assess the insertion site, sutures or securement, dressing, tubing, reservoir compression when prescribed, dependent loops, patency, and the client’s pain and vital signs. Keep collection systems positioned as directed and measure each drain separately. Describe amount, color, consistency, odor when clinically relevant, and trend.

A sudden increase in bright-red drainage with tachycardia or hypotension can indicate bleeding. Sudden cessation accompanied by swelling, pain, leakage, or distention can indicate obstruction or displacement. Protect the client, assess stability, check for an external mechanical problem, and escalate. Do not strip, milk, irrigate, advance, or remove a drain unless the order, device instructions, scope, and policy support the action.

Delegation and communication

Assistive personnel may measure and record output, empty selected collection containers, provide routine hygiene, and report changes when trained and permitted by policy. The RN assesses the client and device, interprets the trend, decides urgency, performs restricted interventions, communicates with the team, and evaluates the response. A reported output is a cue; it does not replace nursing assessment.

Document the whole safety loop

Record the device type and location, indication review, site and skin condition, dressing and securement, external-length or insertion-mark comparison when applicable, patency and prescribed settings, output characteristics and amount, client symptoms and response, infection-prevention care, teaching, action taken, notifications, and reassessment. Avoid charting only “line intact” or “drain normal.”

For example: “1015: Enteral feeding paused after external tube length increased from documented 58 cm to 66 cm following coughing episode. Client awake; respirations 22/min, SpO₂ 95% on room air, no acute distress. Tube secured without advancement; placement-verification pathway initiated and provider notified. No feeding or medication given pending confirmation.”

Clinical example

A client receiving a vesicant infusion reports new burning at the peripheral IV. The RN stops the infusion, assesses swelling and color change, and does not flush. The catheter remains in place while the RN identifies the medication, activates the extravasation protocol, contacts the appropriate provider and pharmacy resource, and prepares for medication-specific aspiration or antidote instructions. The RN documents the findings, treatment, communication, and serial tissue assessment.
